doc.title: Wayne Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Bill Harris, Kai Winding and the advice to go to New York
summary: Bill Harris returned to the band, recommended Andre to Kai Winding, and told him to go into the studios.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Right. He was not a follower?

It wasn’t anything personal, you know. So I finally went to Woody. Because Bill had always played first trombone in that band. And I finally went to Woody and I says, “You know Woody, — maybe it’d be better for the band if Bill plays first trombone and I follow him.” Well it worked and it was great. Except for those new pieces that Bill didn’t know, and then it was a problem with his time because — he had wonderful time but by the time the thing went from here to here to here it came out late because he was an admittedly bad reader. So if he was reading something he knew it was like on the money. But if he was sight reading something it was like — anyways — and Bill was the one that said to me, “Wayne, when I left the band—” and Bill Harris, without telling me this, because Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson were around the corner in Philadelphia. We were working at Pep’s and they were around the corner, I forget the name of that club there, and I didn’t know Kai but Bill certainly did. And it was Bill that recommended me to Kai for his group. So that’s when Kai called me. That’s when I left Woody’s band and Bill Harris said to me he says, “Wayne, the way you read and everything else, whatever you do don’t stay out here, go to New York and go in the studios. Because that’s where you’re going to make the money.”

And he hadn’t been successful at it. He had been — matter of fact he is on some of those Sauter-Finegan studio recordings, Bill Harris, because he was around New York. But he hadn’t been successful at the studio thing only because of his reading, and his individuality too. You know he couldn’t play like Tommy Dorsey. He could only play like Bill Harris. And back in the days in the studios when you first came to New York in the studios and you have to play any kind of written solo it really had to be in the tradition of Tommy Dorsey.
